transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 min (recorded)
Location: Zoom
Notes: demo focused on migration from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API, parity mapping and Console/Optimize walkthrough

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE team walked Asterion Labs through the adapter-based parity approach for switching runtime traffic to Redwood, demoed the Console Studio (routes, rollouts, model variants), and walked cost/latency tradeoffs. Customer asked about KV cache behavior, tokenization differences, function-calling parity, and security controls for Private deployments. Next steps agreed: parity spreadsheet, pilot benchmark, and security pack share.

Topics: parity mapping, tokenization differences, streaming vs webhooks, console rollout policies, dedicated vs hosted economics, pilot benchmarks, SOC2/KMS questions

Transcript:
[00:00:02] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm lena park from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me i have owen ramirez and sofia chen.
[00:00:10] Priya Nair: thanks lena, priya here. we have Marco, Dana, Evan on as well. excited to see how this swap could look.
[00:00:18] Lena Park: great, quick agenda: parity approach, console demo (routes/rollouts), optimize suggestions (batching/quant), then Q&A. we'll try to keep it practical.
[00:00:30] Owen Ramirez: hey all, i can dig into the runtime bits. quick note — if anyone sees a term misheard in the transcript, shout out.

[00:01:02] Sofia Chen: first slide, high-level: many teams we work with keep their calling contract (openai-style REST) and run an adapter that maps to Redwood. that minimizes app change and lets us handle model variant routing, prefix caching, and fallbacks.
[00:01:28] Marco Silva: when you say adapter — is that client-side or edge? we currently have a server-side shim in k8s.
[00:01:35] Owen Ramirez: good q. adapter is flexible — most customers keep it server-side in their k8s cluster. it can be a sidecar or a separate service. key is it translates the few api differences (model name, streaming tokens, function calling payload shape).

[00:02:05] Dana Li: tokenization — our billing is per-token and oai/gpt counts differ from other tokenizers. how do you handle that?
[00:02:13] Owen Ramirez: we surfaced a tokenization diff matrix in the parity spreadsheet, but short answer: Redwood exposes the tokenizer used per model and we provide a token_count endpoint in the console api for exact parity checks. also we run a small preflight that re-tokenizes your sample prompts to estimate delta.
[00:02:45] Lena Park: important for cost forecasting — and we'll show the console panel where you can compare token counts by model variant in real-time.

[00:03:20] [short silence, rustle of papers]
[00:03:35] Sofia Chen: demo time. i'm going to share my screen — navigating to Redwood Console -> Projects -> Asterion-demo.
[00:03:48] [screen share noise]
[00:03:52] Sofia Chen: here is the routes page. route is essentially a logical endpoint. we can map your existing swagger endpoints to routes and pin model versions. notice the "canary" rollout control, traffic split and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if latency exceeds threshold.
[00:04:20] Evan Brooks: that automatic fallback — does it preserve the same response schema? we do a lot of function calling.
[00:04:28] Owen Ramirez: yes, we try to preserve the contract. function calling semantics are supported — we map the function signature and the tool-call/unstructured fields the same way. there are edge cases where model variant lacks tool-call support and we mark that in the variant compatibility table.

[00:05:00] Marco Silva: you mentioned kv cache earlier — curious how that behaves across rolling instances.
[00:05:08] Owen Ramirez: our runtime maintains a per-session KV cache; for high-throughput apps we recommend sticky sessions or a shared cache layer. for Dedicated customers, we provide optimized KV cache migration to avoid cache warm-up when scaling.
[00:05:36] Dana Li: sticky sessions aren't ideal for us — we prefer stateless. any suggestions?
[00:05:42] Owen Ramirez: yes, for stateless architecture we use prefix caching: common prompts that are repeated are cached at a routing layer so tokens are not recomputed. Combine that with batching windows tuned in Optimize and you get stateless scaling with low cold-start overhead.

[00:06:15] [laptop fan hum]
[00:06:33] Sofia Chen: switching to the Parity tab — here's a mapping example from OpenAI-style model names to Redwood model variants. note quantization profiles: q8_0 vs q4f16 etc — we recommend q8_0 for throughput but q4f16 for tight memory constraints.
[00:06:58] Priya Nair: are those quantization profiles automatically evaluated? we care about quality regressions.
[00:07:06] Owen Ramirez: yes, Optimize includes a small quality monitor. we run your prompt set against candidate quantized variants and surface delta metrics (BLEU-like and heuristics for hallucination). the Console flags any variant with >X% regression.

[00:07:40] Lena Park: also, for early pilots we suggest running both host and dedicated comparisons — sometimes the hosted routes are cheaper at low QPS due to multi-tenant economy.

[00:08:05] Marco Silva: streaming support — our client expects chunked JSON deltas. does Redwood streaming map 1:1?
[00:08:12] Owen Ramirez: yes, streaming is supported; adapter maps chunk framing differences. we also support webhooks for server push. important detail: streaming latency is affected by batching window, so we show latency histograms in Console and you can set batching target per-route.

[00:08:55] Dana Li: security — if we go Private/VPC, do you integrate with our KMS? audit logs?
[00:09:03] Lena Park: absolutely. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM, SAML SSO for the console, RBAC roles, and full audit logs. our enterprise pack includes SOC 2 docs and a compliance packet we can share.
[00:09:25] Priya Nair: excellent. could you send those docs after the call?
[00:09:29] Lena Park: yes, i'll include the security pack in the follow-up.

[00:09:58] [transition noise]
[00:10:05] Sofia Chen: demo: i'm going to configure a canary rollout. step 1: create a variant named redwood-gptx-2-q8. step 2: set a latency SLO of 120ms p95 and set fallback to redwood-gptx-1-q4 if SLO breached.
[00:10:25] Marco Silva: do you expose cost per-token by variant in the console?
[00:10:31] Sofia Chen: yes — cost estimation is per-token + per-request amortized infra. the Console shows predicted monthly cost for current traffic patterns; you can toggle quantization and it updates the estimate.

[00:11:05] Evan Brooks: one operational concern — our infra team needs a runbook for degradations and how Redwood falls back to older variants. can you show the logs/audit?
[00:11:14] Owen Ramirez: sure, navigate to Observability -> Routes -> Errors. here you can see trace ids, token counts, routing decisions, and the exact fallback trigger. we also emit events to your tracing stack via OTLP.

[00:11:40] Priya Nair: OTLP is a yes for us. we run jaeger and datadog.
[00:11:45] Owen Ramirez: we have exporters for both.

[00:12:08] [short pause]
[00:12:20] Sofia Chen: switching to the Optimize tab — here's a recommended batching window. based on your traffic pattern (we asked for a sample), Optimize recommends 25ms continuous-batching with a max batch size of 64 for the billing-critical route. this reduces tokens/sec cost by ~18% in our sim.
[00:12:47] Marco Silva: does Optimize provide suggested quantization per workload?
[00:12:52] Sofia Chen: Yes: it ranks variants by cost-quality tradeoff and suggests quant profiles with a confidence score. we also show a canary experiment you can run to validate on live traffic.

[00:13:22] Lena Park: quick live example: i toggled the canary to 10% traffic, the console shows real-time diff for answer time and model score.
[00:13:35] [murmurs]
[00:14:00] Priya Nair: how do you handle embedding parity? our semantic search stacks rely on numeric stability across models.
[00:14:07] Owen Ramirez: embeddings are in the parity sheet — we provide L2/ cosine drift metrics between candidate models; for some customers we keep an "embedding bridge" where we re-embed a small corpus and provide a migration drift report. for high-sensitivity pipelines we recommend a short hybrid window where both embeddings are stored and a reconciliation layer runs.

[00:14:45] Dana Li: that's helpful. what about rate limits — our clients may have bursty traffic and we need predictable 429 behavior.
[00:14:53] Sofia Chen: Redwood has per-route rate limits and queuing strategies. for Dedicated we can configure higher soft-limits and provide SLA-backed throughput.

[00:15:20] [keyboard clack]
[00:15:30] Owen Ramirez: technical deep dive: i want to call out some gotchas we commonly see when porting from Anthropic. Anthropic's safety/response shaping means prompts may need slight tuning. we provide a built-in eval harness to score safety/regulatory prompts.
[00:15:52] Marco Silva: do you run those safety checks automatically during a canary?
[00:15:57] Owen Ramirez: yes, you can attach an eval suite to a rollout and block promotion if safety regressions detected.

[00:16:25] Priya Nair: latency vs cost question — we track p95 tightly for user-facing chat. what's your typical p95 for hosted vs dedicated?
[00:16:33] Lena Park: depends on model and region. typical hosted p95 for a gptx-like family is 90–150ms for small sequence lengths. Dedicated can be lower and more stable — we provide target SLOs in the contract. we'll capture your exact numbers during the pilot.

[00:17:00] Dana Li: pilot — what's included? we want a realistic comparison against our current OpenAI + Together setup.
[00:17:07] Owen Ramirez: Pilot includes: a dedicated test pool (if you want Dedicated eval), or a hosted tenant with reserved concurrency; we run your prompt set across current providers and Redwood variants, collect cost/latency/quality metrics, and deliver a report with recommended variant and quant profile.

[00:17:42] Priya Nair: sounds good. schedule that after we send prompts.

[00:17:55] [soft chuckle]
[00:18:10] Evan Brooks: any code changes for our clients? our SDKs wrap the openai client heavily.
[00:18:18] Sofia Chen: minimal. adapter code samples we provide are drop-in replacements that expose the same endpoints and slightly adapt the streaming frames. we shared a node/python ruby sample in the setup repo.
[00:18:38] Marco Silva: do you support fine-grained response streaming vs full payload? some clients expect partial json fragments.
[00:18:45] Owen Ramirez: yes, partial JSON chunks are compatible; adapter layer can reframe chunks into your expected shape.

[00:19:10] [pause]
[00:19:25] Lena Park: quick pause for any regulatory questions?
[00:19:29] Priya Nair: data residency — we'll need EU-only hosting for certain customers.
[00:19:35] Lena Park: Redwood has EU regions and we can restrict model serving to region and disable cross-region fallback for those routes. this is in the Console under routing -> region policy.

[00:19:58] Dana Li: logging retention — how long do you retain logs in hosted?
[00:20:04] Owen Ramirez: default 30 days for hosted; Dedicated and Private can extend retention; we can also push logs to your S3 for long-term storage.

[00:20:22] [murmur of agreement]
[00:20:40] Sofia Chen: demo wrap: the adapter repo has a sample express server, a python flask shim, and a k8s helm chart. we'll attach link in follow-up.
[00:20:50] Marco Silva: awesome. one more: inference cost delta estimates — how do you calculate across different tokenizers?
[00:20:58] Owen Ramirez: we normalize by token counts after re-tokenizing your corpus with each model's tokenizer, then apply per-token variant price and infra amortization. the parity CSV has line items showing raw tokens, normalized tokens, and projected monthly cost.

[00:21:30] Priya Nair: can you show an example of an actual parity CSV?
[00:21:33] Lena Park: yep i'll share one — in the follow-up you'll see for each route: original provider, token ratio, recommended redwood variant, quant profile, estimated monthly cost.

[00:21:58] [brief laughter]
[00:22:10] Evan Brooks: any customers who did a big swap recently you can namecheck? (we understand NDA limits).
[00:22:16] Lena Park: without getting into specifics, we've run several migrations across health and finance where teams saved 20–40% on unit costs while matching latency. we'll share anonymized case studies.

[00:22:50] Marco Silva: reliability question — we need guaranteed fallback if Redwood is temporarily degraded. what's process?
[00:22:57] Owen Ramirez: we support multi-provider routing: you can configure primary->secondary mapping (e.g., Redwood -> OpenAI) and automatic failover on error rate or latency. the adapter can be configured to keep a short local cache and fall back to previous answers when strict uptime is required.

[00:23:28] [typing]
[00:23:40] Priya Nair: ok, let's talk timeline. we want to decide before end of Q3. pilot in July, decision in August?
[00:23:47] Lena Park: that timeline is feasible. we'll aim for pilot mid-july, 2–3 week evaluation, decision by late august.

[00:24:10] Sofia Chen: question from my side — for Anthropic parity, do you have an automated prompt rewrite?
[00:24:17] Owen Ramirez: we have heuristic rewrites and a small supervised mapping for role prompting differences. it's not magic, but it reduces manual tuning. we ship the rewrites as part of the adapter layer.

[00:24:45] [short pause]
[00:25:00] Marco Silva: will the pilot include embedding drift numbers? that's critical.
[00:25:05] Owen Ramirez: yes, drift is part of pilot reporting — we compute cosine/L2 statistics and sample nearest neighbor deltas.

[00:25:32] Lena Park: ok folks we're getting to wrap. quick recap: lena will share parity spreadsheet + secure docs, owen will stand up pilot, asterion to send prompts and traffic profile.
[00:25:50] Priya Nair: agreed. please include a checklist for infra requirements (k8s config, egress rules).
[00:25:58] Owen Ramirez: we'll include a runbook and a sample helm chart.

[00:26:15] Evan Brooks: one last operational Q — are there tooling hooks for A/B testing answers in the UI?
[00:26:22] Sofia Chen: yes, we have an A/B experiment framework in Console — you can route percentages and the UI shows per-variant scorecards.

[00:26:45] [paper shuffle]
[00:27:00] Marco Silva: small nit: what are default backpressure behaviors if batch queue fills?
[00:27:06] Owen Ramirez: backpressure is configurable: you can drop with 429 or increase batching window to absorb bursts. Console warns on expected latency impact.

[00:27:34] Priya Nair: okay great. let's confirm dates in follow-up email.

[00:27:42] Lena Park: will do — thanks everyone. we'll send follow-up with links, parity CSV, security pack, and proposed pilot dates.
[00:27:55] [call closing small talk]
[00:28:20] [end of recording - remaining minutes were Q&A and scheduling follow ups]
